title: Redwood Edgecases Demo: long context + high TPS + streaming timeouts
topics: High TPS bursts and sustained throughput
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Atlas Health through an edge-cases demo focusing on long-context handling, high TPS scenarios, streaming backpressure and timeouts. transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-11-04
Time: 09:15 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (CTO, Atlas Health), Sara Gomez (ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (Infra), Priya Singh (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete): Demo of edge-case behavior around long contexts, high TPS, streaming backpressure and timeout handling. Several security questions on VPC/KMS/SOC2. Next steps agreed.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, really appreciate you blocking time. I'm Maya, I'll run the demo and Jordan will jump into the deep technical bits.
[00:08] Ravi Patel: Thanks, Maya. We're excited — we have some pretty gnarly edge cases, long conversation histories, and high spike loads.
[00:14] Maya Chen: Great. Quick agenda: high-level demo of the API and Console, then Jordan shows Optimize and serving behavior for long contexts, then we run a short sim of streaming with backpressure and timeouts.
[00:26] Jordan Lee: Hi all, quick note — we'll be using a synthetic dataset that mirrors Atlas's profile, so expect to see long prefix caching, continuous batching, and fallback routing in action.
[00:36] Sara Gomez: Quick question — for context size, we told you 120k tokens as an upper bound, is that right?
[00:41] Jordan Lee: Yep, that's what you communicated. Redwood's runtime supports sharded context windows with prefix KV caching — um, sometimes transcribed as "KV cash" in notes — but the idea is we avoid re-decoding repeated prefixes.
[00:53] Priya Singh: Also curious about streaming — we have a frontend that relies on streaming partial tokens and we can't block more than 2s on the first byte.
[01:00] Maya Chen: Totally. We'll show streaming latency, and the built-in backpressure controls in the Console.
[01:06] Ravi Patel: Security — we need clarity on data residency and KMS since we'll be handling PHI.
[01:11] Maya Chen: Understood; we'll share SOC2 docs and the KMS integration guide. For Private deployment we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations.
[01:20] Jordan Lee: Ok jumping into the Console — (screen share audio) — here's the per-route dashboard, token-level latency heatmaps, and the batch size histogram. For long contexts you'll see cache hit ratios on the right.
[01:38] Maya Chen: Note: we've pre-configured a model variant that is quantized and tuned for long-seq inference — less memory, slightly higher latency per token but much lower cost.
[01:49] Sara Gomez: Are there tradeoffs with hallucination when quantizing?
[01:52] Jordan Lee: Slight risk, yes — Optimize suggests a guard-rail: run regressions on a prompt set, we can pin a higher-precision variant for sensitive routes.
[02:02] Liam O'Connor: For high TPS, what's our recommended deployment? Dedicated or hosted?
[02:08] Maya Chen: If you need sustained high throughput with predictable SLOs, Dedicated is usually best — reserved GPU pools, autoscale to your commit. Hosted can absorb bursts but cost may spike.
[02:19] Ravi Patel: We want burst capacity up to 500 TPS and sustained ~150 TPS during daytime. How does batching affect latency for small short requests versus long context reads?
[02:30] Jordan Lee: Good question — continuous batching increases throughput but for tail latency you can configure priority lanes and latency SLOs. Console shows per-priority latency; we also support request tagging so the dispatcher routes low-latency traffic differently.
[02:44] Maya Chen: Also prefix/KV cache helps long-context workloads: if the token prefix is repeated across sessions, we can reuse cached KV states which reduces compute. But cache population and eviction policy needs tuning depending on distribution.
[02:56] Sara Gomez: Does Redwood persist KV cache across restarts on Private?
[02:59] Jordan Lee: On Private, yes — if you configure persistent volumes. On hosted we persist warm caches across steady traffic; cold restarts will need population.
[03:09] Ravi Patel: Alright, demo the streaming case?
[03:11] Jordan Lee: Sure — switching to the streaming sim. We'll send a long 80k token context and then stream generation back. Note timestamps are rough; the recording can be imperfect.
[03:25] [sfx: brief pause]
[03:28] Jordan Lee: Starting stream. You'll see initial chunk emitted ~600ms after request accept, then we stream subsequent tokens in micro-batches.
[03:37] Priya Singh: That initial chunk is ok but we often care about first byte under 200-300ms. Can you tune that?
[03:43] Jordan Lee: You can — there's a fast-path that sacrifices batching for first-byte latency; Console exposes that knob. But you'll trade off throughput.
[03:52] Maya Chen: For your 2s first byte SLO, we'd recommend hybrid routing: critical routes on low-latency lanes, bulk routes on high-throughput lanes.
[04:03] Sara Gomez: Backpressure — what happens when frontend can't keep up with token rate?
[04:08] Jordan Lee: If the consumer stops reading, the server applies TCP backpressure; Redwood's streaming protocol supports windowing out to the client and an adaptive throttling step — if client read buffer is full we will slow emission and dynamically reduce batch size to avoid OOMs.
[04:23] Ravi Patel: But we saw timeouts in our last PoC — after 30s the gateway dropped the call. How do you handle long-running streams?
[04:30] Jordan Lee: We surface heartbeat chunks and can send partials and checkpoints. For requests that may exceed upstream gateway timeouts, we recommend chunked responses + resumable stream tokens; for Private we can lift layer-7 timeouts.
[04:45] Liam O'Connor: Are resumable streams part of the public API?
[04:48] Jordan Lee: Beta, yes. We can enable for pilots. It allows clients to reconnect and request continuation from a sequence id.
[04:56] Maya Chen: Quick note — we've seen mis-transcribes in some docs where "resumable" got written as "room-able" which, uh, is amusing.
[05:02] [laughs]
[05:05] Sara Gomez: OK, can you simulate a burst?
[05:07] Jordan Lee: Running a load sim now — burst profile: 500 TPS for 30s, sustained 150 TPS. We'll show autoscaling and any queueing/backpressure.
[05:17] [keyboard clacking; load generator audio in bg]
[05:30] Jordan Lee: Alright, metrics — you can see queue depth jump, dispatcher routes to warm nodes; autoscaler spins up dedicated workers after 12s, throughput recovers. There is a small tail-latency bump ~200ms.
[05:46] Ravi Patel: That 12s scale-up looks long for us. Can you shorten?
[05:50] Jordan Lee: Yes — autoscale policy is configurable. For Dedicated you can provision headroom or warm standby. For hosted, warm pools reduce cold-starts but cost goes up.
[06:00] Maya Chen: Also note our burst capacity feature lets you configure short-lived spot blocks to absorb spikes.
[06:07] Priya Singh: About timeouts again — in our infra the load balancer has a 60s idle timeout. If a stream has long gaps, will it get cut?
[06:15] Jordan Lee: By default yes — but workarounds: keepalive heartbeats, chunked responses, or configure the gateway to extend idle time. For Private you can control all that.
[06:25] Sara Gomez: Any examples of customers doing 100k+ tokens in production?
[06:29] Jordan Lee: A couple in healthcare and legal, yes. They either use Dedicated with persistent KV caches or split context into on-disk prefix stores and only warm the frequent prefixes.
[06:40] Ravi Patel: How much does cost change when we enable persistent caches and keep warm nodes?
[06:45] Maya Chen: Roughly you trade compute with storage and headroom; typical numbers: keeping one warm node per 100 sessions might add ~20% to baseline infra cost but reduces per-token compute 30-50% due to cache hits — but we'll run your real numbers in the pilot.
[06:59] Liam O'Connor: For compliance — do you have audit logs per request and token-level tracing?
[07:04] Jordan Lee: Yes, Console has per-request tracing hooks and we export audit logs to your S3 or SIEM. On Private you can route logs into your own retention.
[07:12] Priya Singh: KMS integration details?
[07:15] Maya Chen: We'll share the KMS guide. We support AWS KMS and custom HSM via KMIP in Private.
[07:22] Sara Gomez: If we do a pilot, what would success criteria look like?
[07:25] Ravi Patel: For us: 1) first byte < 2s for critical routes, 2) no data egress violations and KMS in place, 3) sustained 150 TPS for 24h with acceptable cost.
[07:35] Maya Chen: Great, we'll bake those into the pilot success metrics.
[07:40] Jordan Lee: Quick demo of a timeout scenario — I'm going to artificially slow downstream consumption to simulate client-side backpressure.
[07:47] [pause, synthetic load noise]
[07:55] Jordan Lee: You can see Console marks the stream as "throttled" and applies adaptive batching; after 35s the gateway started to drop idle connections in this sim — that matches what you saw earlier, Ravi.
[08:07] Ravi Patel: So the fix is to either extend gateway idle time or enable resumable streams?
[08:11] Jordan Lee: Exactly. Resumable streams let you reconnect and continue.
[08:15] Priya Singh: Any limitations on resumable streams with long contexts?
[08:19] Jordan Lee: You need to checkpoint the KV state periodically; we keep checkpoints per session but very large contexts may need segmented checkpoints. It's doable but we'll prototype with your dataset.
[08:28] Sara Gomez: About SDKs — do you support streaming in Node/Python with built-in reconnection logic?
[08:33] Jordan Lee: Yes, SDK includes sample reconnection snippets; for more advanced behavior we'll share a small client library.
[08:40] Maya Chen: Time check — about 20 minutes left. Any other hot topics?
[08:44] Ravi Patel: Regarding model variants — we need to keep an LLM with higher precision for PHI redaction tasks. Can you do automatic fallback?
[08:52] Jordan Lee: Yes — routing policies can automatically fallback to a higher-precision variant if the lower-precision model fails a regression. Optimize can run the eval suite and trigger rollbacks.
[08:59] Priya Singh: Can you demo Optimize quickly?
[09:02] Jordan Lee: Sure — Optimize suggests quantization profiles, batching windows, and gives cost vs latency tradeoff charts. Here we show a chart comparing 8-bit quantized variant vs fp16: you get ~2x cost improvement but slight tail-latency and occasional quality deltas.
[09:20] Sara Gomez: If quality drops, can we do route-based guarding?
[09:23] Jordan Lee: Yep — route-level pinning and canary rollouts; you can run A/B and auto-fallback on regression-induced score drops.
[09:30] Maya Chen: Wrapping up — recap and next steps?
[09:33] Maya Chen: We'll send pilot proposal and pricing. Jordan will provision a test harness for a 120k token + 500 TPS burst sim. Atlas will share traffic patterns and SSO/KMS constraints. We'll schedule a 2h kickoff next Wed.
[09:46] Ravi Patel: Sounds good. Also please attach SOC2 and the KMS/HSM integration doc.
[09:50] Maya Chen: Will do.
[09:52] Priya Singh: One last ask — can you include sample dashboards for per-route token latency?
[09:56] Jordan Lee: Yep, attaching a sample dashboard link in the follow-up.
[09:59] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, appreciate it. We'll follow up with action items.
[10:03] Ravi Patel: Thanks all.
[10:05] [meeting ends]

Notes about transcription: occasional mis-hearings ("KV cash" / "room-able"), speaker overlap and filler words retained.
